rationale: Start with a broad organic range to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds and reveal retention and resolution bottlenecks. A moderate gradient duration and midpoint temperature provide a useful baseline for subsequent optimization.
Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin survives. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate gradient steepness.
Test higher temperature to change selectivity in the tightly spaced central cluster while retaining the fast gradient. This may recover baseline resolution without introducing a time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the remaining under-resolved pair at 55 C. The last peak should still elute near the zero-time-penalty window, while this run tests whether the central cluster retains adequate separation.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient for additional resolution margin. Keeping temperature fixed should preserve selectivity, while the last peak is expected to remain near the zero-time-penalty window.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, test whether a 5 C increase improves the marginal central-pair resolution while shortening retention. Keep the gradient identical to injection 4 to isolate temperature-dependent selectivity.

Return to the successful 55 C temperature and test a slightly higher starting organic fraction. This probes whether retention can be shortened while preserving full resolution and the maximum CRF already achieved.

Slightly flatten injection 7's gradient to improve its sole under-resolved pair while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. The observed trends suggest this could restore full resolution with the last peak still below 8 minutes.

Further flatten the gradient slightly to lift the remaining R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. The last peak is projected to elute near 8 minutes, potentially matching the maximum CRF with a larger minimum-resolution margin.

Test 5 C below injection 4 to assess temperature sensitivity around the maximum-scoring method. This complements the 60 C result and checks whether full resolution and zero time penalty persist at a lower temperature.

Test a higher starting organic fraction paired with a shallower gradient to improve the central resolution margin while offsetting the longer gradient's retention cost. The maximum CRF is already secured; this explores an alternative method near the same time window.

Explore a substantially faster gradient at 60 C to test whether the near-coeluting central pair separates after an elution-order reversal. This probes a different selectivity regime for a shorter maximum-scoring method, while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as benchmarks.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the fast gradient to seek another fully resolved method. The last peak may remain within the zero-time-penalty window, while stronger temperature shifts could separate the central cluster differently.

Preserve injection 4's successful gradient slope and temperature while ending the programmed ramp earlier at lower organic content. All peaks previously eluted before this ramp would end, so this method should retain the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Maintain the maximum-scoring gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint further. The gradient reaches the outlet through 8.65 minutes, after the observed last peak at 7.60 minutes, so the separation should remain unchanged.

Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to target full resolution with a last-peak time below 8 minutes. This may match the maximum CRF while balancing the two limiting pairs more evenly than injection 4.

Keep the successful initial gradient slope but transition to a 50% organic hold after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether a lower endpoint can retain full resolution and keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

Slightly flatten injection 9's gradient to increase separation of its R = 1.67 pair while checking that the other limiting pair remains above 1.5. Injection 17 shows that zero time penalty extends beyond 8 minutes, providing room to test this alternative maximum-scoring method.

Flatten injection 11's gradient to improve its R = 1.10 pair while retaining the stronger separation of the other central pair. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can provide a larger resolution margin without a time penalty.

Reduce the gradient slope modestly from injection 19 to bring its remaining R = 1.41 pair above 1.5. The last peak is projected near 9 minutes, testing whether this higher-starting-organic method can also achieve the maximum CRF.

Use a slope between injections 9 and 18, both of which achieved CRF 1.000, while restoring the high-organic endpoint. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty with more retention-time margin than injection 20.

Preserve injection 9's maximum-scoring gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 60% organic. The ramp should still encompass all peak elution, so this tests a lower-endpoint alternative expected to retain CRF 1.000.

Test a slightly shallower gradient and lower endpoint than injection 22. Nearby results suggest full resolution may persist, with the last peak still inside the approximately 9-minute zero-time-penalty window.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 16 to locate the faster edge of the fully resolved region. This may sacrifice some resolution, but it checks whether a shorter alternative can match the already-achieved maximum CRF.

Finish with a gradient slope bracketed by the maximum-scoring injections 18 and 21. This untested method is expected to preserve full resolution and zero time penalty, matching the campaign's already-achieved maximum CRF of 1.000.
